chapter_metadata.title: Cricothyroidotomy
key_points: Cricothyroidotomy is the quickest route to stabilize the airway when intubation fails.
Surgical airway is the endpoint of difficult airway algorithms.
In children <10–12 years, needle cricothyroidotomy is preferred; convert to tracheostomy as soon as feasible.

definitions.content: Cricothyroidotomy is the creation of a surgical opening through the cricothyroid membrane and placement of a tube for ventilation.

structures.name: Cricothyroid (CT) membrane
structures.notes: Incise lower half to avoid branches of cricothyroid artery.

structures.name: Cricothyroid artery
structures.notes: Usually traverses superior half of CT membrane; small branches penetrate membrane.

structures.name: Thyroid cartilage / cricoid cartilage
structures.notes: CT membrane lies between; vocal folds ~10 mm above superior aspect of CT membrane.

structures.name: Anterior jugular veins
structures.notes: Avoid by vertical midline skin incision.

structures.name: Thyroid isthmus
structures.notes: Typically below level of CT membrane dissection.

technology_and_technique.summary: Needle (temporizing in adults), open surgical, rapid 4‑step technique (faster but more complications in models), and percutaneous Seldinger‑based; operator training drives success.
Vertical midline skin incision; horizontal incision in lower half of CT membrane; use tube OD ≤8 mm; confirm with CO₂ and breath sounds.
Prefer needle cricothyroidotomy if <10–12 years; avoid surgical cricothyroidotomy; convert to tracheostomy early.

clinical_procedures.name: Needle cricothyroidotomy (temporizing, adults)
steps: Identify CT membrane via midline palpation; alternative: 3–4 fingerbreadths above suprasternal notch with neck neutral.
Use large-bore catheter-over-needle (e.g., 14-g) attached to syringe partially filled with saline/water.
Advance at ~45° angle caudally through skin and CT membrane while aspirating; air bubbles confirm entry.
Withdraw needle, leave cannula; connect oxygen tubing.
Deliver oxygen at 10–12 L/min; use Y-connector to allow periodic CO₂ release.
clinical_procedures.notes: In adults, inadequate ventilation for CO₂ clearance—use only as a bridge to surgical cricothyroidotomy or tracheostomy.

clinical_procedures.name: Open surgical cricothyroidotomy (standard)
steps: Prep anterior neck from mandible angle to sternal notch; maintain sterile technique; position with mandible anteriorly displaced.
Stabilize larynx with thumb and long finger; use index finger to palpate and reidentify CT membrane throughout.
Make a 2 cm midline vertical skin incision over CT membrane, staying strictly in midline to avoid anterior jugular veins.
Palpate CT membrane through incision and make a horizontal incision in the lower half of the membrane.
Insert cricoid hook and apply gentle upward traction on cricoid; avoid traction on thyroid to protect vocal folds.
Dilate cephalocaudally using Trousseau dilator or Kelly clamp to enlarge the opening.
Insert tested tracheostomy or endotracheal tube (outer diameter ≤8 mm) at ~90° between dilator blades; rotate counterclockwise to seat against the neck.
Confirm placement with end-tidal CO₂ return and bilateral breath sounds; secure tube to neck with suture.
clinical_procedures.notes: Equipment bundle: scalpel no. 15; hemostats ×2; cricoid hook; 14-g needle + cannula, 6-cc syringe; Trousseau dilator/Kelly; cuffed no. 4 trach tube; cuffed no. 5 ETT; gauze; Betadine; drapes.

clinical_procedures.name: Rapid 4‑Step Technique (RFST)
steps: Operator at head of bed; identify landmarks and stabilize.
Horizontal stab incision through skin, subcutaneous tissue, and CT membrane to access airway.
Stabilize larynx by hooking cricoid cartilage; apply upward traction.
Insert tracheostomy tube as per standard technique and confirm placement.
clinical_procedures.notes: Approx. one‑third the time of standard technique in cadaver trials, but higher complication rate (e.g., cricoid fractures).

clinical_procedures.name: Percutaneous (Seldinger-based) cricothyroidotomy
steps: Small vertical skin incision over CT membrane; stabilize larynx with nondominant hand.
Advance 18‑gauge needle with syringe through CT membrane; aspirate air to confirm airway entry.
Insert guide wire; remove needle without dislodging wire.
Advance cannula/dilator over wire into airway; seat cannula; remove dilator and wire.
clinical_procedures.notes: Ease for non‑surgeons familiar with wire‑guided access; literature shows mixed results vs. open technique (complications/time/success vary by operator experience).

diagnostic_approaches.name: ASA Difficult Airway Definition
criteria_or_scoring: “the clinical situation in which a conventionally trained anesthesiologist experiences difficulty with face mask ventilation
diagnostic_approaches.interpretation: If difficulty with mask ventilation or tracheal intubation occurs, classify as a difficult airway.
diagnostic_approaches.when_to_use: When assessing airway difficulty in patients
diagnostic_approaches.source_excerpt: A difﬁcult airway is “the clinical situation in which a conventionally trained anesthesiologist experiences difﬁculty with face mask ventilation, difﬁculty with tracheal intubation, or both” [1].

diagnostic_approaches.name: Palpation via thyroid notch to identify cricothyroid membrane
diagnostic_approaches.purpose: Identify the cricothyroid membrane for airway access
criteria_or_scoring: Located inferior to thyroid cartilage border and superior to cricoid cartilage
diagnostic_approaches.how_to_perform: Slide a finger down the thyroid cartilage to identify the membrane position between cartilages.
diagnostic_approaches.interpretation: Membrane is identified when palpated between thyroid and cricoid cartilages.
limitations: In patients with significant neck edema or trauma
diagnostic_approaches.when_to_use: Before cricothyroidotomy to locate the CT membrane
diagnostic_approaches.source_excerpt: sliding a ﬁnger down the thyroid cartilage, the cricothyroid membrane can be identiﬁed just inferior to the border of this cartilage and superior to the cricoid cartilage

diagnostic_approaches.name: Alternative landmark: suprasternal notch distance to CT membrane
diagnostic_approaches.purpose: Estimate CT membrane location when landmarks are difficult to palpate
criteria_or_scoring: Suprasternal notch is typically three to four fingerbreadths below the CT membrane
diagnostic_approaches.how_to_perform: Use suprasternal notch and measure three to four fingerbreadths upward with the neck neutral.
diagnostic_approaches.interpretation: CT membrane lies three to four fingerbreadths above the suprasternal notch.
diagnostic_approaches.when_to_use: When edema, trauma, or obesity obscures anterior neck landmarks
diagnostic_approaches.source_excerpt: An alternative landmark is the suprasternal notch, which is typically three to four ﬁngerbreadths below the CT membrane with the neck in neutral position.

diagnostic_approaches.name: Syringe aspiration air bubbles to confirm CT membrane puncture
diagnostic_approaches.purpose: Confirm airway entry during needle cricothyroidotomy
diagnostic_approaches.how_to_perform: Advance needle at a 45° angle pointing inferiorly; aspirate to detect air bubbles after passing the CT membrane.
diagnostic_approaches.interpretation: Air bubbles in the syringe indicate entry into the airway.
diagnostic_approaches.when_to_use: During needle cricothyroidotomy to verify placement
diagnostic_approaches.source_excerpt: advanced through the skin at a 45° angle pointing inferiorly. When the needle pushes through the CT membrane, aspiration will reveal air bubbles within the syringe.

diagnostic_approaches.name: Three-finger laryngeal stabilization and CT membrane palpation
diagnostic_approaches.purpose: Locate and reidentify the CT membrane during surgical cricothyroidotomy
diagnostic_approaches.how_to_perform: Immobilize larynx with thumb and long finger; use index finger to palpate and reidentify the CT membrane.
diagnostic_approaches.interpretation: Tactile confirmation of CT membrane location.
diagnostic_approaches.source_excerpt: the larynx is ﬁrmly immobilized by the thumb and long ﬁnger, with the index ﬁnger free to palpate, locate, and reidentify the cricothyroid (CT) membrane

diagnostic_approaches.name: Palpation of cricothyroid (CT) membrane through incision
diagnostic_approaches.purpose: Reconfirm CT membrane position before proceeding
diagnostic_approaches.how_to_perform: Index finger palpates the CT membrane through the incision while larynx is pinned in midline.
diagnostic_approaches.when_to_use: After skin incision while stabilizing larynx.
diagnostic_approaches.source_excerpt: the index finger palpates the CT membrane through the incision, reconfirming its position and planning the following steps.

diagnostic_approaches.name: Capnography (CO2 return) to confirm tube placement
diagnostic_approaches.purpose: Confirm proper placement of tracheostomy or endotracheal tube
diagnostic_approaches.how_to_perform: Use monitoring equipment to detect CO2 return.
diagnostic_approaches.when_to_use: Before securing tube to neck with suture.
diagnostic_approaches.source_excerpt: proper placement should be confirmed by both the presence of CO2 return on the monitoring equipment and successful auscultation of breath sounds.

diagnostic_approaches.name: Auscultation of breath sounds to confirm tube placement
diagnostic_approaches.purpose: Confirm proper placement of tracheostomy or endotracheal tube
diagnostic_approaches.how_to_perform: Auscultate for breath sounds after tube insertion.
diagnostic_approaches.when_to_use: Before securing tube to neck with suture.
diagnostic_approaches.source_excerpt: proper placement should be confirmed by both the presence of CO2 return on the monitoring equipment and successful auscultation of breath sounds.

diagnostic_approaches.name: Aspiration of air via syringe during percutaneous cricothyroidotomy
diagnostic_approaches.purpose: Confirm proper needle position within the airway
diagnostic_approaches.how_to_perform: Introduce an 18-gauge needle with syringe through the CT membrane; confirm by aspirating air.
diagnostic_approaches.when_to_use: During percutaneous cricothyroidotomy after landmark identification and laryngeal fixation.
diagnostic_approaches.source_excerpt: an 18-gauge needle attached to a syringe is introduced through the CT membrane, and proper positioning is confirmed with aspiration of air.

diagnostic_approaches.name: Point-of-care ultrasound to identify the cricothyroid membrane
diagnostic_approaches.purpose: Identify CT membrane anatomy prior to cricothyroidotomy
diagnostic_approaches.how_to_perform: Use handheld point-of-care ultrasound in the emergency setting.
diagnostic_approaches.source_excerpt: Using point-of-care ultrasound can identify the cricothyroid membrane prior to cricothyroidotomy and potentially decrease complications.

diagnostic_approaches.name: Flexible endoscopy or formal bronchoscopy after surgical access
diagnostic_approaches.purpose: Examine the airway for causes of obstruction
diagnostic_approaches.how_to_perform: Perform flexible endoscopy or formal bronchoscopy after access is stabilized.
diagnostic_approaches.interpretation: Identifies airway pathology; reversible causes can then be addressed.
diagnostic_approaches.source_excerpt: the airway should be examined either by flexible endoscopy or formal bronchoscopy.

diagnostic_approaches.name: Postoperative chest x-ray
diagnostic_approaches.interpretation: Identifies presence or absence of pneumothorax or pneumomediastinum.
diagnostic_approaches.source_excerpt: Postoperative chest x-ray is important to rule out pneumothorax or pneumomediastinum.

clinical_guidelines.title: Emergency difficult airway endpoint
specific_recommendations: If inability to intubate AND ventilate is determined, proceed immediately to surgical airway.
Avoid repeated intubation attempts that increase morbidity and mortality.

clinical_guidelines.title: Pediatric airway selection
specific_recommendations: Age <10 years: surgical cricothyroidotomy is strongly contraindicated.
Age <10–12 years: prefer needle cricothyroidotomy with percutaneous transtracheal ventilation; convert to tracheostomy as soon as feasible.

clinical_guidelines.title: Elective candidacy (avoid)
specific_recommendations: Avoid elective cricothyroidotomy after prolonged intubation (>5–7 days).
Avoid if laryngeal inflammation/infection or history of laryngeal trauma is present.
Consider tracheostomy as alternative for long‑term access.

clinical_guidelines.title: Relative contraindications
specific_recommendations: Severe neck trauma/edema or expanding neck hematoma (landmarks obscured).
Known upper tracheal pathology—consider lower tracheostomy if anatomic barrier exists.

clinical_guidelines.title: Intra‑procedure safety
specific_recommendations: Vertical midline skin incision to avoid anterior jugular veins.
Horizontal incision through LOWER half of CT membrane to avoid cricothyroid artery branches.
Use tube with outer diameter ≤8 mm; confirm with CO₂ and auscultation before securing.

clinical_guidelines.title: Postoperative management
specific_recommendations: Examine airway with flexible endoscopy/bronchoscopy for reversible causes.
Obtain postoperative chest x‑ray to rule out pneumothorax/pneumomediastinum.
Initiate tracheostomy‑style tube care: humidification, inner cannula cleaning, suctioning, cuff‑pressure monitoring, skin care.
If access anticipated >48–72 h, consider conversion to tracheostomy; evidence for routine conversion is mixed.

complications: Early: failure to establish airway, hemorrhage, aspiration, pneumothorax, pneumomediastinum, esophageal perforation, vocal fold injury, laryngeal disruption.
Long‑term: laryngotracheal stenosis, aspiration, dysphagia, dysphonia (voice change), TE fistula, infection, delayed hemorrhage, laryngo‑cutaneous fistula, tracheomalacia, tube obstruction.
clinical_presentation: Inability to intubate and ventilate; upper airway obstruction (trauma, edema, burns, foreign body, stenosis, extrinsic compression).
management: Surgical airway is endpoint of difficult airway algorithms; do not delay once inability to intubate and ventilate is established.
Technique selection depends on age, anatomy, operator expertise, and available equipment.
Postoperative care mirrors tracheostomy care; consider conversion to tracheostomy when prolonged access is anticipated (>48–72 h).

summary: In a cannot‑intubate/cannot‑ventilate scenario, proceed directly to surgical airway.
Adults: select open vs percutaneous technique based on training and availability; needle cricothyroidotomy is a bridge.
Children <10–12 years: perform needle cricothyroidotomy and convert to tracheostomy promptly.
After airway secured, confirm with CO₂ and auscultation; obtain chest x‑ray and initiate tube/skin care; consider conversion to tracheostomy if >48–72 h.

subglottic_stenosis.notes: Risk higher with elective cricothyroidotomy in the presence of laryngeal inflammation or after prolonged intubation.

incorrect_tube_placement.notes: Historic reports cite misplacement through the thyrohyoid membrane as a cause.

increases: Incision into superior half of CT membrane
decreases: Horizontal incision in lower half of CT membrane

prognosis: When performed promptly by trained operators, high success with acceptable complication rates; risk rises with delays and misplacement.

points: Cricothyroidotomy is rapid, effective, and often life‑saving when intubation fails.
Complication rates are acceptable when performed by trained operators and compare favorably with emergency tracheostomy.
Elective use requires careful selection; avoid when laryngeal inflammation or prolonged intubation is present.

references.citation: Tracheostomy, while still preferred for long-term airway management, has a higher complication rate than cricothyroidotomy when performed on an emergent basis and thus should be performed in a more controlled setting [16].
references.key_findings: Emergent tracheostomy has a higher complication rate than cricothyroidotomy; should be done in a controlled setting.
references.source_excerpt: higher complication rate than cricothyroidotomy when performed on an emergent basis ... controlled setting [16].
